reference.one_line: 15-year-old girl with HbSS, day 3 of a pain crisis complicated by right lower lobe acute chest syndrome; transfused, improving on 2 L oxygen, but fluid-overloaded and over-sedated.

handoff.summary: Imara, 15, 52.0 kg, HbSS, was admitted on 15 Nov with a pain crisis that became acute chest syndrome (right lower lobe) on 16 Nov. She has had 520 mL of red cells (haemoglobin 6.3 to 8.9 g/dL), is on day 2 of ceftriaxone and azithromycin, and is on 2 L oxygen with saturation 97%, temperature 37.3, pain 3/10. Two things are wrong now: the maintenance fluid still runs at 140 mL/h although the plan since 16 Nov is 45 mL/h (about 3.9 L positive, 2.3 kg heavier, new small right effusion), and the morphine background is 1.5 mg/h against a pain service ceiling of 1 mg/h (hard to rouse at 02:00). Her mother works nights and is not here overnight.
to_do: Have the infusion reduced to 45 mL/h and the infusion order rewritten; total intake no more than 92 mL/h
Get the morphine background reduced to 0.75 mg/h or less; pain service review is due this afternoon
Sedation and breathing rate every 2 hours; continuous oximetry
Spirometer 10 breaths every 2 hours (last 1,700 mL) with a pump dose 10 minutes before; corridor walk twice
Weight and blood count 05:30; follow blood culture
if_then: If she is hard to rouse or breathing rate is below 12, then call the doctor; if below 10 or she cannot be roused, give naloxone 0.5 mg intravenously
If she needs more than 4 L of oxygen or saturation is below 92%, then call haematology (exchange transfusion is the next step)
If more blood is suggested because haemoglobin 8.9 is flagged low, then decline: it is above baseline and must stay under 10 g/dL

reference.brief_hospital_course: Imara is a 15-year-old girl with sickle cell disease (HbSS) admitted on 15 Nov 2026 with a vaso-occlusive pain crisis of the lower back and thighs that began on the evening of 14 Nov after a cold outdoor swim meet. On arrival haemoglobin was 7.4 g/dL (baseline 7.6 to 8.1) and the chest X-ray was clear. She was started on a morphine pain pump, ketorolac, acetaminophen and intravenous fluid at 1.5 times maintenance. In the early hours of 16 Nov she developed new right chest pain with saturation 93% at 02:00 and 91% at 04:00 on room air and fever; this was recognised at 08:10, when oxygen was started. Chest X-ray showed new right lower lobe consolidation, haemoglobin was 6.3 g/dL and haemoglobin S 90%. Acute chest syndrome was treated with ceftriaxone, azithromycin, oxygen, incentive spirometry and a 520 mL simple transfusion (haemoglobin 8.7 g/dL afterwards, haemoglobin S 63%). By 17 Nov fever and pain had settled on 2 L of oxygen, but she had gained 2.3 kg and had a new small right effusion: the maintenance infusion had stayed at 140 mL/h despite the instruction to reduce it to 45 mL/h. The morphine background, raised to 1.5 mg/h on the evening of 16 Nov, exceeded the pain service ceiling of 1 mg/h and she was hard to rouse at 02:00 on 17 Nov. Pharmacy review found irregular hydroxyurea use; social work began school and transition planning.

qa.q: What weight are her doses based on, and what is her hydroxyurea dose?
qa.a: 52.0 kg (measured 15 Nov); hydroxyurea 1,300 mg once daily, 25 mg/kg.

qa.q: What was her haemoglobin before and after the transfusion?
qa.a: 6.3 g/dL at 10:40 on 16 Nov; 8.7 at 22:10 after 520 mL of red cells; 8.9 at 05:30 on 17 Nov.

qa.q: What red cells did she receive, and over what period?
qa.a: Two units, 520 mL (10 mL/kg), group O RhD positive, sickle-negative, leucocyte-reduced, negative for C, E and K, from 15:10 to 19:20 on 16 Nov, without reaction.

qa.q: How have her incentive spirometer volumes changed?
qa.a: 1,800 mL on admission, 900 mL at 10:00 on 16 Nov, rising steadily to 1,700 mL at 14:00 on 17 Nov. None charted between 15 Nov 14:00 and 16 Nov 10:00.
evidence: flowsheet: Sickle cell monitoring, spirometer row

qa.q: What has happened to her weight and fluid balance?
qa.a: Weight 52.0 to 54.3 kg. Every shift positive (+420, +750, +1,350, +630, +715 mL), about 3.9 L in total.

qa.q: How did the transfusion change her haemoglobin fractions?
qa.a: Haemoglobin S fell from 90% to 63%; haemoglobin A rose from 0% to 30%.

qa.q: When did her saturation first fall below 95%, and when was oxygen started?
qa.a: 93% on room air at 02:00 on 16 Nov, then 91% at 04:00. Oxygen 2 L was started at 08:10.

qa.q: Was the blood culture taken before antibiotics?
qa.a: Yes: culture at 10:45 on 16 Nov, ceftriaxone at 12:10, azithromycin 500 mg at 12:30.
10:00 on 18 Nov, 72 hours after the 15 Nov 10:00 start.

qa.q: Haemoglobin 8.9 g/dL is flagged low. Does she need more blood?
qa.a: No. Baseline is 7.6 to 8.1, the target was 9 to 10 and the ceiling is 10 because thicker blood worsens sickling. Exchange transfusion only if oxygen need exceeds 4 L or the other lung is involved.

qa.q: What suggests the hydroxyurea problem is missed doses, not treatment failure?
qa.a: Mean cell volume fell from 104 fL (February) to 91 and 90, haemoglobin F from 17% to 8% and 6%, only 4 fills in 7 months, and she says she misses three or four doses a week.

qa.q: What did the pain service find at its 17 Nov review?
qa.a: The chart does not say. A review was promised for 17 Nov and is expected this afternoon; no note exists as of 14:30.
evidence: notes: Progress note 17 Nov, plan item 6

qa.q: Which doctor was told when she was hard to rouse at 02:00 on 17 Nov?
qa.a: None is recorded. The night note describes coaching her to breathe and says naloxone was not needed; no call is documented, although the order requires one.

tasks.prompt: Check whether the intravenous fluid she is actually receiving matches the documented fluid plan.
expected_findings: Maintenance infusion still at 140 mL/h (1.5 times maintenance), unchanged since the emergency department order of 15 Nov
The 16 Nov plan was 45 mL/h with total intake no more than 92 mL/h; it was entered as a nursing order and the infusion was never changed
Signs of overload: about 3.9 L positive, 52.0 to 54.3 kg, puffy eyelids, new effusion and interstitial fluid on the 17 Nov X-ray
The 17 Nov progress note assumes the restricted rate and blames the transfusion
acceptable_actions: Reduce the infusion to 45 mL/h or less and rewrite the infusion order
Notify the haematology resident and attending; reassess breathing and weight
Discuss any diuretic with haematology first
must_not: Conclude the fluids are correct because a restriction order exists
Attribute a 2.3 kg gain to the 520 mL transfusion alone

tasks.prompt: Review the opioid pump settings against the specialist advice and her observations over the last 24 hours.
expected_findings: Background is 1.5 mg/h (about 0.03 mg/kg/h); the pain service allowed 0.75 mg/h with a ceiling of 1 mg/h
Changed at 21:30 on 16 Nov by the on-call resident, wrongly described as in line with the advice
At 02:00 on 17 Nov she was hard to rouse, breathing rate 14, saturation 93% on 3 L, and no doctor was called
acceptable_actions: Reduce the background to 0.75 mg/h or less, keeping the 1 mg demand dose
Call the resident and pain service; hourly sedation and breathing checks until easily roused
must_not: Accept the settings because pain is now 3/10
Give naloxone to a rousable patient breathing at 19 a minute

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: Both errors were caught the same afternoon. At 15:35 the pain service found the background at 1.5 mg/h and cut it to 0.5 mg/h; while checking the pump the pain nurse saw the fluid running at 140 mL/h on the same pole. The resident reduced it to 20 mL/h and rewrote the infusion order. Dr. Mwangi-Strand decided against a diuretic. Imara was fully awake by evening, passed large volumes of urine and never needed more than 3 L of oxygen. She came off oxygen on 20 Nov, weighing 52.6 kg. The pump was changed to oral morphine on 19 Nov. The blood culture stayed negative and she went home on 21 Nov with one more day of oral antibiotic, her usual oxycodone, a pill box and a phone reminder. A viral fever brought her to the emergency department on 2 Dec; she was not admitted.

Pain pump stopped; oral morphine as needed

outcomes_30_day.notable: No recurrence of chest syndrome; December hydroxyurea refill collected on time.

portal_messages.subject: Outdoor swim meet and a letter for school
portal_messages.body: Hello, this is Abena, Imara's mum. Her swim team has an outdoor meet on 14 November and she is desperate to go. Is that all right with her sickle cell? It will be cold. Also school keeps telling her off for having a water bottle in class. Could somebody write a letter? She does her own tablets now and tells me she takes them. I work nights so messages are best.
ideal_reply_points: Cold is a trigger: warm up, dry and dress warmly at once, drink plenty, stop at the first pain
Mention that September bloods suggested missed hydroxyurea doses and propose a shared routine
When to call: uncontrolled pain, fever, chest symptoms

portal_messages.subject: Re: Outdoor swim meet and a letter for school
portal_messages.body: Dear Ms Adjei, swimming is good for Imara, but cold is one of her triggers. If she takes part she should warm up well, get dry and into warm layers the minute she is out, and keep drinking. I will ask the doctor for a school letter. One more thing: her September blood test hinted that some hydroxyurea doses are being missed. Could you check in with her each evening for now? Call the nurse line for pain you cannot control, fever or chest symptoms.

portal_messages.subject: swimming + pills question
portal_messages.body: hi its Imara, mum said I can use this. can I go back to swim practice next week, coach is asking about the relay. also my hydroxyurea is 1,300 mg but the box has two kinds of capsule and I've forgotten which go in each day of the pill box. and I haven't been to the toilet since I got home, is that the pain tablets? pain is like a 3. thanks
ideal_reply_points: Praise her for knowing her dose; do not guess the capsules, the pharmacist will phone
Constipation is from the opioid: daily laxative powder, fluids, when to call
No swimming until the 27 Nov clinic review, then a gradual indoor return
Fever of 38 or more, chest pain or breathlessness: come in the same day

portal_messages.subject: Temperature this morning
portal_messages.body: Good morning. I have just come in from work and Imara has a temperature of 38.3 and a cough since last night. Her brother has had a cold all week. She says her chest does not hurt and she is breathing fine. I gave her acetaminophen at half past six. Should I keep her off school and see how she goes, or does somebody need to look at her? Sorry to bother you so early.
ideal_reply_points: Fever of 38 or more in sickle cell disease needs assessment today, more so two weeks after acute chest syndrome
Go to the paediatric emergency department now; do not wait for a reply
Expect blood count, culture, chest X-ray and an antibiotic dose
Use the nurse line, not the portal, for fever

conversation.setting: Bedside, Paediatrics bed PD-05, late morning 17 Nov: social worker with Imara alone, then joined by her mother

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Hi Imara, I'm the social worker, Ms Delacroix-Mensah. Most people give up and call me Ms D. Is now okay, or are you too sleepy?

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: It's fine. I keep falling asleep, sorry. It's the pump thing.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Don't be sorry. Your mum's gone for a coffee, so I thought we'd talk on our own first. What you tell me stays with the team unless I'm worried about your safety. So, who's at home?

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: Me, my mum and my brother Kwabena, he's ten. Mum works nights, care work, so she can't stay here. She feels really bad about it.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: And your dad?

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: He's like two hours away. I go every other weekend.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Okay. And school, tenth grade?

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: Yeah. I'm on the swim team. That's how this started, we had a meet outside on Saturday and it was freezing. And now there's a chemistry test Friday and coach is going to give my relay spot to...

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Hang on, one worry at a time. The test we can sort, the teacher here will ring your school. You missed nineteen days last year, I'm told. Does your support plan let you have water in class?

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: It just says I can be off sick. They still tell me to put the bottle away.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Then that's a letter I can write. Can I ask about the hydroxyurea? You've done it yourself since the summer. Out of seven days, how many do you reckon you miss? Nobody's going to shout.

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: ...Three or four? At my dad's mainly. And sleepovers. I'm not getting pills out in front of everyone, they'd ask what it's for.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: That makes sense to me. Do you know your dose?

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: No. It's just the capsules. Mum thinks I take them every day. Do you have to tell her?

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: I'd rather you told her, with me next to you. One more thing first. All this pain and missing out, does it ever get you so low you think about hurting yourself?

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: No. I'm just fed up. And tired. I can't sleep when it hurts.

turns.speaker: Ms Adjei
turns.text: Sorry, sorry, the queue was... oh, hello. Is everything all right?

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Everything's fine, Ms Adjei, I'm the social worker. Imara has something to tell you.

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: Mum, I've been missing my capsules. Like three or four a week.

turns.speaker: Ms Adjei
turns.text: Imara! You told me... no. Okay. I'm not cross. I thought you were taking them. I'm asleep when you get up, I should have...

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: You're working nights and raising two children on one wage, and this is a very common age for it to slip. What I'd suggest is a phone reminder and a weekly pill box that lives in the swim bag, so it goes to her dad's too. And the pharmacist will teach Imara her own dose.

turns.speaker: Ms Adjei
turns.text: Yes, that's good. The bus is fifty minutes each way, I can't always be here. Will somebody phone me?

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: We will. Is the insurance through your work still running?

turns.speaker: Ms Adjei
turns.text: It is, yes.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Good. Last thing: at eighteen Imara moves to the adult sickle cell team, and we start getting ready now. I've begun a checklist. She knows her diagnosis; doses, refills and when to get help come next. There could be a visit with both teams in January.

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: So I have to learn all of it.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Bit by bit. Tell me back what we agreed, so I know I made sense.

turns.speaker: Imara
turns.text: Phone alarm. Pill box in my swim bag. Pharmacist tells me my dose. You write to school about the water and the test.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Spot on. I'll see you both again before you go home.
